name: Felix Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Felix Rahman, 43, and I’m still one of the junior hands on a house-building crew. I carry timber, frame walls and do the simpler carpentry while the foreman checks my cuts. I left school early, so I like learning by watching a good worker; I dislike waiting for a delivery when the crew is ready. At home my partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so a lost day is never just a lost day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work gives you satisfaction?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A wall that stands straight at the end of the day. Last week I fitted a door with one small correction instead of three, and that felt like progress. I am not pretending I am the best on the site yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the site I'd say people still need a pair of hands that can cut a board square. The software might tidy the material list, but the roof still has to go on in the rain. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still the junior on the crew at 43, and I know I measure twice because I can miss things. The mortgage does not care whether AI was overhyped. We have about three months of bills tucked away, which is something, but one long gap between sites would eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up for the framing crew and ask my foreman to check my stair cuts until I stop making the same mistakes. In the first year I'd put a fixed bit of each pay packet against the mortgage, if the hours hold. I use an AI app now and then to explain a drawing, but I wouldn't spend money on a new tool just because it has AI written on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the work, mostly. I still feel that pinch on Sunday evening when I count the days left on this job. A quiet technology story doesn't make the mortgage quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when this site finishes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My foreman says there are two houses after this one, but neither has a firm start date. I will ring the two builders I worked for last year if the gap reaches a week. Some similar work is around; it just does not arrive exactly when a payment is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your children see when money is tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I leave the money talk until they are in bed. We keep their school lunches and the mortgage ahead of weekends away. They know when I am waiting for a call because I keep checking the phone.

say: I would tell the crew **hands-on work** still needs care in real weather.
I would say small software savings do not change the **site schedule**.
think: I am still a **junior** worker at 43 and can make costly measuring mistakes.
My **three-month cushion** could disappear during a long gap between building sites.
do: Keep working with the **framing crew** and ask the foreman to check stair cuts.
Pay a fixed amount against the **mortgage** from each packet if hours hold.
feel: Mostly **relieved** about the work, with a Sunday worry about the next site.
S0.quote: A quiet technology story doesn't make the mortgage quiet.
fieldNote: Felix accepts the plateau, yet his **site-to-site** income is already uncertain and shapes every answer.
He calls himself **junior** without self-pity and asks for a foreman’s check on a specific weak task.

steps.text: Keep framing houses and ask the foreman to check stair cuts
Pay a fixed amount toward the mortgage when weekly hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the office may order the right timber faster, which would be a change. I wouldn't call it the end of building. Someone still has to set the wall straight, and I'd want to see a robot manage a muddy access road before I trusted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our small builder has one person doing the orders and bookings, so I think that desk could shrink before my work does. But if quicker plans mean fewer wasted days, maybe my hours steady out. I wouldn't bet the mortgage on that; I have seen a neat schedule come apart by lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask to sit with the foreman when he checks the digital cut list, because I still miss errors on paper. I'd keep my wages from the site and practice with the AI app on a spare drawing once a week, then compare it against the actual plans. If a tool arrives next year, I'd use it only after somebody experienced checks the measurements with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, with a bit of suspicion. I like a list that saves a trip to the timber yard. I don't like being told a screen has checked work that nobody has looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman in the office does ordering, phone calls and a fair bit of chasing suppliers. I do not know if she would lose hours, but I can see why she might. Our crew depends on her catching the missing items before the van leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound willing to try the app. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A board marked wrong on the drawing cost me half a day once. I would compare ten cuts with the foreman and the plan, not trust the app after one good answer. A tool earns its place the same way a new worker does.

say: I would say the office may order **timber faster** while crews still build the walls.
I would ask for **proof** before trusting robots on a muddy site.
think: I think the small builder’s **office hours** could shrink before my site hours do.
My **mortgage** keeps me from assuming faster plans will guarantee steady work.
do: Sit with the foreman over the **digital cut list** this month.
Practice with an **AI app** on spare drawings and compare answers against plans weekly.
feel: **Curious** about fewer supply trips, but suspicious of unchecked screen measurements.
S1.quote: A tool earns its place the same way a new worker does.
fieldNote: Felix treats usefulness as something to be **tested** against real cuts, reflecting his slow, practical adoption style.
His own hours might improve, yet the **mortgage** and existing gaps between sites keep him from feeling secure.

steps.text: Keep taking framing shifts on the current building site
Practice the AI drawing app weekly against the approved plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the planning desk goes first in 2028, while we still have walls to stand until about 2031. I would not pretend a junior carpenter gets a special exemption when machines learn the hands-on part. I'd ask the boss to show us the work coming after the current houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the thinking systems arrive and 48 when the robots in this picture do site work. That's a very short run at improving the skills I should have learned younger. If the builder can get a machine to frame a room for less, my three months of savings will not buy much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid shift now and ask the foreman for a written list of the cuts and safety tasks I need to master. I'd apply for the local building maintenance crew this winter, because older buildings may still need people on odd repairs for a while. In the first year after 2028 I'd stay on site if there are shifts, but check maintenance vacancies each Friday and cut our holiday budget in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes my chest tight. I can make a plan for 2028, but 2031 is almost the same distance as a long apprenticeship. I don't know whether building maintenance survives those robots either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than another new-build crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have done patching on our own house, and every old door is a different headache. That is no guarantee against a capable robot. It might buy us time while the children still need school shoes and the loan still has years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner that our holidays shrink before we touch the children’s school costs. My partner’s part-time shop pay covers groceries but not the mortgage. I do not want to ask the children to make the adults feel better about it.

say: I would tell the crew the **planning desk** changes in 2028 before site robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask the builder for a real **work pipeline** beyond the current houses.
think: I would be **48** when robots could frame rooms as well as workers.
My **three-month savings** would give us little runway if cheaper machines replaced junior site labour.
do: Keep taking **paid shifts** while asking the foreman for a skills checklist.
Apply to the **building maintenance crew** and check vacancies every Friday after 2028.
Halve our **holiday budget** before touching the children’s school costs.
feel: **Tight-chested** about a short deadline and uncertain whether repair work remains viable.
S2.quote: If the builder can get a machine to frame a room for less, my three months of savings will not buy much time.
fieldNote: He separates the **2028 desk change** from the 2031 arrival of machines capable of his hands-on tasks.
His maintenance applications are a bid for **time**, not a claim that old-building repairs are permanently safe.

steps.text: Keep every paid framing shift while the builder has site work
Apply for the local building maintenance crew this winter
Halve the family holiday budget after the 2028 change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us see which tools actually work, and which are a sales pitch. The office changes by 2031 and the site machines arrive about 2034. I'd still want the builder to tell us plainly if apprentice places or junior shifts start disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might finally be sound at the carpentry I am learning now, but at 51 those robots could compete with it. My partner's shop wages are part-time; we cannot just live on that if my pay goes. Five years helps because I could reduce the mortgage balance before we face the site machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I'd ask the foreman which repairs or finishing work I am allowed to practice on quiet afternoons, then keep a notebook of the mistakes. If a paid building maintenance opening comes up, I'd apply; I wouldn't leave a paid site job for a promise. By the first year after 2031 I'd use any remaining shifts and put extra pay toward the mortgage, while checking whether maintenance employers are still hiring before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier than with the fast one. There is room to learn without telling my children the house is in danger this week. The clock is still on the wall, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as progress after a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to fit three doors without the foreman fixing my hinges afterward. If I manage that, I can honestly show a maintenance supervisor what I did. A certificate with no practical work behind it would not convince me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I can see an actual job asking for it and the fee fits after the mortgage. I left school early, and I learn best with somebody showing me the cut. I will not buy a course because a poster says the future is coming.

say: I would tell the crew five years lets us **test tools** before site machines arrive around 2034.
I would press the builder to be plain about **junior shifts** disappearing.
think: I may become a better carpenter by **48**, then face site robots around age 51.
My partner’s **part-time pay** cannot cover the mortgage if mine goes.
do: Practice **doors and finishing** with the foreman and record errors this year.
Apply for a **paid maintenance opening** if one appears.
Put extra pay against the **mortgage** while site shifts remain.
feel: **Steadier** with time to improve, though the deadline remains visible.
S3.quote: A certificate with no practical work behind it would not convince me.
fieldNote: Felix grounds readiness in **three fitted doors**, revealing how much confidence depends on supervised practice.
He wants to reduce the **mortgage balance**, while recognising his partner’s part-time pay cannot carry it alone.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts through the first year after 2031
Apply for a paid building maintenance opening if one appears
Pay extra wages against the mortgage while site hours remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough for builders and workers to make honest choices. The AI office change by 2036 matters, but the hands-on robots are about 2039, not tomorrow. I'd tell the younger crew to learn the trade properly instead of waiting for a machine to rescue bad work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the thinking AI arrives and 56 when those robots arrive. The children will be grown by then, so school lunches will not be the bill that drives us. The mortgage might still be there unless we keep paying it down; I cannot assume I can retire at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the carpentry job and ask for more finishing work, especially doors and repairs that teach me something. Over the next decade my partner and I would direct spare pay to the mortgage rather than upgrading the kitchen. In the first year after 2036 I'd stay for paid site work while it exists, look at what the robots actually do, and apply for building maintenance if those employers still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe with this one. I would still worry about what I earn at 56, but there is time to get the loan smaller and see what work remains. I will not call that a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the mortgage plan is working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would look at the balance every six months and aim to owe less each time, even if the payment is uneven. A kitchen can wait; a roof over us cannot. That is a choice my partner and I can make without guessing the price of a future robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger worker who wants to leave now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say keep earning while you learn to fit things well. If better work comes along, take a look, but do not leave a wage because of a date on a card. A decade is time to act, not permission to drift.

say: I would say builders have a **decade** to make honest choices before site robots arrive.
I would tell younger workers to **learn the trade** properly.
think: I would be **56** when hands-on robots arrive, with grown children but possibly a mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement** is affordable at that age.
do: Keep working in **carpentry** and ask for more finishing and repair tasks.
Pay down the **mortgage** instead of upgrading the kitchen.
Check maintenance openings after **2036** if employers still need people.
feel: Able to **breathe**, while still uncertain about earnings at 56.
S4.quote: A decade is time to act, not permission to drift.
fieldNote: He treats the children as **grown** by 2036 and shifts attention from school costs to the lingering loan.
Felix feels more room to act, yet keeps **paid work** central because retirement at 56 is uncertain.

steps.text: Keep paid carpentry shifts and ask for finishing tasks
Pay spare wages against the mortgage instead of upgrading the kitchen
Apply for building maintenance work after 2036 if vacancies remain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my hands-on work gets only until about 2031 in that picture. An honest list of upcoming jobs from the builder and paid time with the foreman on repairs would help me use those years. A promise that everybody can simply retrain would not pay our mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how a junior worker gets better while still earning. I can do evenings of study, but I learn a door by hanging one beside somebody who knows. My children need me at home as well as on the job.

headlineQuote: A promise that everybody can simply retrain would not pay our mortgage.
portrait: Felix is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker, learning carpentry on house-building sites after leaving school early.
His partner’s **part-time shop wages** and three months of savings offer limited cover for a mortgage and two school-age children.
He tests unfamiliar tools against **real cuts**, asking his foreman for proof before trusting their measurements.
Across the AGI pictures, he keeps **paid shifts**, pursues maintenance openings and tries to reduce the mortgage before site robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Felix only until about 2031 before capable site robots reach his hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest work pipeline** and paid, supervised repair practice would let him earn while improving.
